props.title: Attack and Retreat
props.initialSlug: When retreat is not an option.

sections.content: **Attack and Retreat (1964)** (1964), also known as "Italiani brava gente," stands as a remarkable Italian-Soviet co-production that offers a unique perspective on WWII's Eastern Front. Director Giuseppe De Santis crafts a haunting portrait of Italian soldiers fighting alongside German forces in the Soviet Union, similar to the way Stalingrad (1993) and **Cross of Iron** (1977) examine the brutal Eastern Front campaign. The film's unflinching portrayal of the Italian military's disastrous Russian campaign parallels other notable WWII Italian perspectives like **General Della Rovere** (1959) and **Two Women** (1960).

sections.content: The film's power lies in its authentic depiction of the Italian soldiers' gradual disillusionment, moving from initial fascist propaganda-fueled confidence to the stark reality of warfare in the brutal Russian winter. Like Come and See (1985) and **The Cranes Are Flying** (1957), it captures the psychological toll of the Eastern Front through a combination of intimate character moments and sweeping battle sequences.

De Santis's neo-realist background influences the film's raw authenticity, similar to Roberto Rossellini's war trilogy, particularly **Rome, Open City** (1945). The joint Italian-Soviet production allows for a balanced perspective rarely seen in war films of this era, presenting both sides with humanity while acknowledging the historical complexities of the conflict. sections.content: **Attack and Retreat** (1964) helped pave the way for more nuanced examinations of the Eastern Front, influencing later works like **Enemy at the Gates** (2001) and **Life and Fate** (2012). Its focus on the human cost of war, particularly through the lens of Italian soldiers fighting in an unfamiliar land, creates a unique narrative that stands apart from typical Allied or Axis perspectives of WWII cinema.
